issues.legal_issue: A codicil must satisfy the same execution and proof requirements as the will to which it relates.
material_facts: The disputed instrument was a statement made in connection with registration of an already executed will and was conceded to be capable of amounting to a codicil.
The statement purported to alter the will by limiting the beneficiary’s interest and providing for the property to pass to others after her death.
issues.conclusion: A codicil must be executed and proved in the same manner as a will; the disputed codicil was not proved and could not alter the will.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(b), 63, 64 and 70 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, read with Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, support applying the same execution and proof rules to a codicil as to a will. A codicil forms part of the related will and alters its dispositions; it would be anomalous to require formal execution and proof of a will but not of an instrument that changes it.

predicates.codicil_execution_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a purported codicil was validly executed and proved.
predicates.codicil_relates_to_will: The instrument explains, alters, or adds to dispositions made in a will.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a codicil related to a will, the codicil must meet the same execution and proof formalities as the will.

issues.legal_issue: A registrar may qualify as an attesting witness only by performing the acts of attestation and proving them in testimony; registration alone is insufficient.
material_facts: The registrar recorded the testator’s statement and signed below it, but also performed official registration duties.
The registrar and the other person whose signature appeared on the statement were not examined in court to prove attestation.
issues.conclusion: A registrar does not become an attesting witness merely by registering a testamentary instrument. A registrar may qualify if the registrar attested in the legally required manner, but that attestation must be proved through the registrar’s testimony; it was not proved here.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an attesting witness must see the testator sign or receive the testator’s personal acknowledgment and sign in the testator’s presence. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, informs the requirement that a witness sign with the intention of attesting. M.L. Abdul Jabhar Sahib v. H.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons, [1969] 3 SCR 513, explains that signing for another purpose does not constitute attestation. Dharam Singh v. Aso, [1990] Supp. SCC 684, and Beni Chand v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar, [1977] 1 SCR 578, are also considered. A registrar’s testimony may establish that the registrar acted as an attesting witness, but the registrar’s official act of registration alone does not.

rule.if: testamentary_attestation_dispute and registrar_saw_execution_or_received_acknowledgment and registrar_signed_in_testator_presence and registrar_signed_with_attesting_intent and registrar_testified_about_attestation

predicates.testamentary_attestation_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a will or codicil was duly attested.
predicates.registrar_saw_execution_or_received_ackn: The registrar saw the testator sign or received the testator’s personal acknowledgment of the signature.
predicates.registrar_signed_in_testator_presence: The registrar signed the instrument in the testator’s presence.
predicates.registrar_signed_with_attesting_intent: The registrar signed to attest the testator’s signature, rather than solely to perform an official registration function.
predicates.registrar_testified_about_attestation: The registrar testified in court about the events establishing attestation.

issues.definition: In a dispute about testamentary attestation, a registrar qualifies as an attesting witness only if the registrar performed the acts of attestation with that intention and testified about them.

issues.legal_issue: Registration of a will or codicil does not replace proof of its execution and attestation where the law requires attestation.
material_facts: The will and the disputed codicil were registered.
The will’s execution and attestation were admitted, but the execution and attestation of the codicil were disputed.
No attesting witness to the codicil was examined in court.
issues.conclusion: Registration and the registrar’s endorsements did not dispense with the need to prove the codicil’s execution and attestation in the manner required by law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, requires a document that must be attested to be proved through at least one available attesting witness; a will is excluded from the registration-based dispensation described in the proviso to that section. Sections 52, 58, 59 and 60 of the Registration Act, 1908, govern the registrar’s endorsements and certification. Section 114, illustration (e), of the Evidence Act permits a presumption that official acts were regularly performed, but the registration endorsements concern registration and do not establish attestation. Kunwar Surendra Bahadur Singh v. Thakur Behari Singh, AIR 1989 PC 117, is relied on for the limited relevance of those endorsements.

predicates.registered_testamentary_instrument_proof: The proceeding concerns proof of a registered will or codicil.
predicates.instrument_requires_attestation: The instrument is one that the law requires to be attested.

issues.definition: For a registered testamentary instrument that must be attested, registration does not replace proof of execution and attestation.

issues.legal_issue: A codicil is not proved when no attesting witness is examined to establish its execution and attestation, and an unproved codicil cannot alter an admitted will.
material_facts: The execution and attestation of the original will were admitted.
The disputed codicil was the testator’s recorded statement that departed from the will’s terms.
Neither person whose signature appeared in connection with the codicil was examined to prove its execution and attestation.
The appeal challenged the dismissal of a civil claim to title and consequential relief based on the alleged effect of the codicil.
issues.conclusion: The codicil was not proved and could not alter the will. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, require the execution and attestation of a codicil to be proved as they would be for a will. Registration does not remove that requirement, and a registrar’s endorsement does not itself prove attestation.

rule.if: civil_title_case_based_on_codicil and will_execution_and_attestation_admitted and codicil_execution_or_attestation_disputed and no_attesting_witness_examined

predicates.civil_title_case_based_on_codicil: The proceeding is a civil title case in which a party relies on a codicil to affect rights under a will.
predicates.will_execution_and_attestation_admitted: The parties admit that the related will was duly executed and attested.
predicates.codicil_execution_or_attestation_dispute: A party disputes whether the codicil was duly executed or attested.
predicates.no_attesting_witness_examined: No attesting witness is examined to prove the codicil’s execution and attestation.

issues.definition: In a civil title case relying on a codicil, if the will is admitted but the codicil is disputed and no attesting witness proves it, the codicil remains unproved and cannot alter the will.
